docs.title: System architecture
docs.text:
racecar firmware

flowchart TB
    Driver([Driver])
    VBUS(["Vehicle CAN · shared bus · 500 kbit/s"])
    PBUS(["Powertrain CAN · shared bus · 500 kbit/s"])

    DASH[Dashboard<br/>screens and buttons]
    FC[Front controller<br/>global governor]
    LV[LV controller<br/>power sequencing]
    TMS[TMS<br/>temperature and fan]
    EXT[BMS · IMD · GPS · Raspberry Pi]

    DASH --- VBUS
    FC --- VBUS
    LV --- VBUS
    TMS --- VBUS
    EXT --- VBUS

    FC --- PBUS
    INV1[Left inverter] --- PBUS
    INV2[Right inverter] --- PBUS

    Driver -->|buttons| DASH
    Driver -->|pedals, brake, steering| FC
    LV -.->|enables power and inverter switch| FC
    FC -.->|enables dashboard power| DASH

    classDef control fill:#c22a00,color:#fff,stroke:#842000
    class FC control

The vehicle bus is a single shared bus: every node hears every vehicle message, and each node decides which messages it cares about. The front controller is the only ECU that transmits on the powertrain bus; the Raspberry Pi logger also listens to both buses.

Most CAN IDs follow a convention that encodes a message class, an ECU number and, for periodic messages, a command/status/alert type. The DBC files define the exact payloads.

docs.title: Four ECUs, two CAN buses
docs.text: The car is controlled by four STM32 boards. They share one vehicle CAN bus; the front controller also sits on a second powertrain CAN bus for the two inverters. Every board runs its own application, and logical control and status coordination happens through CAN messages.

docs.title: The four boards
docs.text:
Board Main job MCU CAN Front controller (FC) Brain of the car: decides when HV and motors may run; sequences contactors; reads driver inputs; computes torque; talks to both inverters STM32F767 Vehicle + powertrain LV controller (LV) Powers up the other boards and subsystems; controls inverter supply and switch; TSSI; cooling; brake light; current sensing STM32F767 Vehicle Dashboard Driver interface: LVGL screens, two physical buttons, profile selection and live telemetry STM32F469 Discovery Vehicle TMS Reads six accumulator thermistors; reports temperatures to the BMS; computes cooling-fan duty STM32F767 Vehicle

External devices on the vehicle bus include the BMS, IMD, GPS and a Raspberry Pi for logging and flashing. The two AMK inverters are on the powertrain bus and are not implemented in this repository.

docs.title: How a start request travels
docs.text:
1. The driver selects a profile on the dashboard and confirms it.
  2. The dashboard sends its screen state in DashStatus over vehicle CAN.
  3. The front controller's global governor reads that state and commands its accumulator state machine to enable HV.
  4. The accumulator sends ContactorCommand to the BMS; the BMS closes the contactors and reports Contactor_Feedback and pack voltage back.
  5. Once HV is running, the dashboard asks to start motors. The front controller starts both inverters, the LV controller closes the shared inverter switch, and the front controller enters RUNNING when the brake is pressed.

The detailed sequence and all governor states are on Startup and the global governor.

docs.title: What each board owns
docs.text:
No board writes another board's GPIO. Ownership is split by physical function:

Output or decision Owner When HV and motors may run; when torque is allowed Front controller Opening and closing the three HV contactors Front controller commands; BMS executes Inverter enable, speed and torque setpoints Front controller Dashboard power, ready-to-drive sound, IMD/BMS warning LEDs Front controller GPIO Power to FC, LV peripherals, accumulator electronics, inverter supply LV controller GPIO Shared inverter switch LV controller GPIO, requested by FC Brake light, TSSI, cooling pumps and fans, HSD current sensing LV controller Screen, buttons, driver profile Dashboard Accumulator temperature reporting and fan speed TMS

The hardware shutdown circuit is separate from all of this software. A shutdown-circuit event removes power directly; it does not wait for a CAN message or a governor state.

docs.title: CAN communication
docs.text:
All coordination between boards happens over two classic CAN buses, both configured for 500 kbit/s:

Bus Nodes Purpose Vehicle Dashboard, front controller, LV controller, TMS, BMS, IMD, GPS, Raspberry Pi Driver requests, power state, contactors, temperatures, telemetry Powertrain Front controller, left inverter, right inverter, Raspberry Pi (logger, receive-only) Inverter enable, speed/torque setpoints, inverter feedback

The front controller is the bridge between the two control domains: it reads driver and dashboard inputs from the vehicle bus and sends motor commands on the powertrain bus.

docs.title: How message IDs are built
docs.text:
The DBC header documents an intended ID convention:

Digit Meaning First 1 special, 2 periodic, 3 sensor, 4 debug Second ECU the message belongs to, not always the sender: 0 front controller, 1 LV controller, 2 TMS, 3 dashboard, 4 Raspberry Pi Third (periodic only) 0 command, 1 status, 2 alerts

Many IDs follow it: FcStatus is 201 (periodic, front controller, status), LvCommand is 210 (periodic, belongs to the LV controller, sent by the FC), DashCommand is 230 (sent by the FC, belongs to the dashboard), LvAlerts is 212, and Accumulator_Soc is 300 (sensor, front controller).

The convention is not enforced. Some periodic frames use the third digit for another purpose: FcCounters is 203, TMSValues is 204, InverterSwitchCommand is 213, and LvDcdc is 214. InverterStatus (241) fits the 2x1 shape but is sent by the FC to the dashboard. TuningParams (340) fits 3xn but carries configuration, not sensor data.

The 1570–1574 block is a separate BMS command/status range: 1570 is FC-sent and 1571–1574 are BMS-sent. Always decode by the DBC message name and signals, not by the ID digits alone.

The BMS, IMD and GPS add 11-bit frames outside this convention. The TMS sends its thermistor broadcast, BmsBroadcast, as a 29-bit extended frame (0x1839F380). The DBC also defines ThermistorBroadcast (0x18FEF1FE) as a second 29-bit frame, but the current application does not send it.

docs.title: Main message flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    DASH[Dashboard] -->|DashStatus| FC[Front controller]
    FC -->|DashCommand| DASH

    FC -->|ContactorCommand| BMS[BMS]
    BMS -->|Contactor_Feedback<br/>Pack_State · Pack_SOC| FC

    FC -->|LvCommand<br/>InverterSwitchCommand| LV[LV controller]
    LV -->|LvStatus · LvAlerts| FC

    FC -->|Inv1/2_Setpoints1| INV[Inverters]
    INV -->|Inv1/2_ActualValues1/2| FC

    TMS[TMS] -->|BmsBroadcast| BMS
    TMS -->|BmsBroadcast| DASH

The arrows show message flow, not physical wiring. All vehicle-bus nodes are attached to the same shared bus.

The most important startup messages are:

Message Sender → receiver Rate Purpose DashStatus Dashboard → FC ~50 Hz Screen state and selected profile DashCommand FC → dashboard 10 Hz Acknowledge startup steps, speed, SOC, reset ContactorCommand FC → BMS 100 Hz Positive, negative and precharge contactor requests Contactor_Feedback BMS → FC/LV/dashboard External Inverted open/closed feedback Pack_State BMS → FC and dashboard External Pack voltage and current Pack_SOC BMS → FC External State of charge and maximum pack voltage InverterSwitchCommand FC → LV 100 Hz Request to close the shared inverter switch LvStatus LV → FC 10 Hz LV state and switch acknowledgment Inv1/2_Setpoints1 FC → inverters 100 Hz Enable bits, speed and torque limits Inv1/2_ActualValues1/2 Inverters → FC External Readiness, speed, current, temperature, error FcStatus FC → Pi 10 Hz Governor, accumulator and motor states LvAlerts LV → FC/dashboard/Pi 10 Hz IMD, BMS and HSD fault flags

LvCommand, sent by the FC at 100 Hz, carries the brake-light request. Its receipt is also how the LV controller knows the FC is online. The exact bit layout and every signal are defined in projects/veh.dbc and projects/pt.dbc.

docs.title: Generated C++ types
docs.text:
The DBC files describe the wire format. scripts/cangen turns them into C++ classes for each ECU:

flowchart LR
    DBC[veh.dbc / pt.dbc] --> GEN[cangen]
    CFG[project config.yaml<br/>node = FC, LVC, TMS or DASH] --> GEN
    GEN --> HDR[Inc/generated/can/<br/>*_bus.hpp · *_messages.hpp]
    HDR --> APP[Src/app.cc]

Each project gets only the messages it sends or receives. For example, the FC gets vehicle and powertrain headers; the TMS gets only the vehicle bus.

The generated bus provides:

VehBus veh_can{can_base};

veh_can.Send(tx_message);

auto latest = veh_can.GetRxDashStatus();   // latest value, retained
auto cleared = veh_can.PopRxDashStatus();  // latest value, then clear

docs.title: Latest value, not a queue
docs.text:
CAN reception is a one-message mailbox per message type. A new frame replaces the previous frame of that type.

  • GetRx...() returns the latest decoded value and keeps it.
  • PopRx...() returns it and clears the slot.
  • There is no automatic age check or timeout.

This is the most common source of confusion when reading startup code:

has_value() does not mean the sender is alive

A dashboard that sent DashStatus once and then stopped still leaves a valid value in the mailbox. The front controller will keep reading that last state unless the application adds its own timeout. Most startup paths do not add one.

The accumulator is the main exception: it pops Pack_State and Pack_SOC and invalidates pack voltage if no matching pair arrives for more than 500 ms.

docs.title: Frames, signals and binary values
docs.text:
These are classic CAN buses, not CAN FD. A frame carries at most 8 data bytes and is identified by an 11-bit or 29-bit ID. The ID names the message, not a destination: every node on the bus sees the frame. Most messages here use 11-bit IDs; the thermistor broadcast from the TMS uses a 29-bit extended ID.

A DBC file describes how the bits inside each frame are interpreted:

  • the message ID, length and sender;
  • each signal's start bit, width, byte order, signedness, scale, offset, range and unit;
  • names for enumerated values.

A signal stores a raw integer. The physical value is:

physical = raw × scale + offset

For example, BppsPercent has scale 0.1 and unit percent. Two details matter in this repository:

  • State numbers are part of the DBC. The FC governor state value 1 is not used; WAIT_DRIVER_SELECT is 2.
  • Units are not always what the name suggests. The dashboard's > 0.20 brake check is 0.20 percentage points, not 20 percent.

docs.title: Watching the bus
docs.text:
With a SocketCAN adapter and the repository checked out:

cd projects
bash monitor_veh.sh    # vehicle bus, can1, veh.dbc
bash monitor_pt.sh     # powertrain bus, can0, pt.dbc

These scripts configure the interface with ip and open cantools monitor. They require Linux, iproute2 and cantools. The Linux interface names are a local convention; they are not the STM32 CAN peripheral numbers.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: The dashboard is the driver interface: an STM32F469I Discovery board running LVGL 9.3 on a 4-inch display. It uses two physical buttons, SCROLL and ENTER, instead of a touchscreen. The board reports its current screen state and selected profile over vehicle CAN; the front controller decides what happens next.

docs.title: One loop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Read buttons] --> B[Update active screen]
    B --> C[Apply global Reset]
    C --> D[Rebuild screen if state changed]
    D --> E[lv_timer_handler]
    E --> F[Send DashStatus]
    F --> G[Delay 20 ms]

The loop period is the 20 ms delay plus the work, so the dashboard runs at roughly 50 Hz rather than a guaranteed 50 Hz. DashStatus contains a wrapping 8-bit counter, the screen state and the selected profile.

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text:
The two inputs are active-low GPIOs. InvertedDigitalInput turns a low electrical level into a logical press.

  • A new level is accepted only if at least 200 ms have passed since the previous accepted edge.
  • The first update takes the current level as a baseline and suppresses both edges.
  • Each button exposes PosEdge(), NegEdge(), IsPressed() and GetHeldDuration().

This is edge spacing, not a requirement for 200 ms of stable input. A held button at boot produces no press edge.

docs.title: Reset
docs.text:
After the active screen updates, Display::Update() checks DashCommand.Reset. If it is true and the dashboard is not already in SELECT_PROFILE, the pending transition is replaced with SELECT_PROFILE and the screen is rebuilt.

This is the only ordinary way back to profile selection after driving.

docs.title: Running screen
docs.text:
The running screen has three columns:

Column Content HV Pack current arc, pack voltage, state of charge Thermals BMS low/high temperature, motor and inverter temperatures LV LV battery voltage/current, FC status, CAN indicator, speed

The current arc is a 100-sample moving average of Pack_State.Pack_Current. The speed comes from DashCommand.Speed. Most numeric labels are integer-truncated. The speedometer is labeled km/h, but the DBC value is in mph and the screen does not convert it. The HV voltage label can also be wrong above 255 V because the FC truncates that field to 8 bits before sending it.

Some indicators are decorative

The FC: OK label is a constant, and the green CAN indicator does not monitor traffic. A disconnected ECU can leave its last value on screen because the dashboard does not check message age.

docs.title: CAN inputs
docs.text:
Message Dashboard use DashCommand Reset, startup acknowledgments, precharge percent, speed, SOC BppsSteerDebug Brake qualification before motor start FcAlerts Raw bit indices on the error screen BmsBroadcast Battery min/max temperature InverterStatus Motor and inverter temperatures Accumulator_Soc Pack voltage and state of charge Pack_State Pack current LvDcdc LV voltage and current (the LV application does not currently send it)

There is one physical vehicle bus. The dashboard reaches it through CAN1; the front controller reaches the same bus through CAN2. The dashboard configuration also requests powertrain headers, but the application does not create a second bus or send on the powertrain bus.

docs.title: Brake threshold
docs.text:
The dashboard's motor-start screen compares BppsPercent() with 0.20. BppsPercent has DBC scale 0.1 and unit percent, so this is 0.20 percentage points, not 20 percent. Raw values 0 and 1 decode to 0 and 0.1 and fail; raw value 2 decodes to a float slightly above 0.20 and passes, as do higher values.

The front controller uses a separate brake check for entering RUNNING: its own brake sensor must read above 10%.

docs.title: Error and shutdown limitations
docs.text: The dashboard does not consume DashCommand.Errored or HvShutdown, and no normal screen transition enters ERROR. The error screen can display bit indices and can request shutdown if entered, but the ordinary driver flow has no path to it. The running screen has no shutdown button action.

docs.title: Front controller
docs.text:
The front controller (FC) is the brain of the car. It owns the global governor, sequences the high-voltage contactors, reads the driver's pedals and steering, computes torque, and runs the two AMK inverter state machines. It also exchanges status with the LV controller and publishes telemetry that the Raspberry Pi logger records.

The FC is the only vehicle ECU that transmits on both CAN buses:

  • Vehicle CAN (CAN2) — dashboard, LV, TMS, BMS, telemetry.
  • Powertrain CAN (CAN1) — left and right inverters.

It works with the other boards:

  • Dashboard — sends the driver's requested startup step and receives acknowledgments.
  • LV controller — supplies FC power and controls the inverter supply and shared switch.
  • Raspberry Pi — logs CAN telemetry and can request ECU flashing; it does not command HV or torque.

docs.title: What runs when
docs.text:
Src/app.cc creates three FreeRTOS tasks after initialization:

Task Period Priority Work task_100hz 10 ms 3 Read sensors; check pedal plausibility; run global governor; update accumulator, vehicle dynamics and motors; send contactor, brake-light, switch and inverter commands task_10hz 100 ms 2 Toggle debug LED; mirror LV fault LEDs; check DBC hash; read suspension and HSD current; send FcStatus, DashCommand, alerts and debug frames task_1hz 1000 ms 1 Send FcGitHash

main() also drives dashboard power high once at boot. The dashboard stays powered as long as the FC has power.

docs.title: Global governor
docs.text:
The governor is the top-level startup state machine. It is documented in full, with its transition table and dashboard handshake, on Startup and the global governor.

In one sentence: the dashboard sends a requested screen state, and the governor turns that request into accumulator and motor enable commands, a torque permission, and a ready-to-drive sound.

docs.title: Accumulator
docs.text:
The accumulator object owns the three contactor commands and validates the BMS feedback. Its state is reported in FcStatus.AccumulatorState.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> IDLE
    IDLE --> STARTUP_ENSURE_OPEN: command ENABLED
    STARTUP_ENSURE_OPEN --> STARTUP_CLOSE_NEG: all feedback open
    STARTUP_CLOSE_NEG --> STARTUP_HOLD_CLOSE_NEG: negative closed
    STARTUP_HOLD_CLOSE_NEG --> STARTUP_CLOSE_PRECHARGE: 100 ms
    STARTUP_CLOSE_PRECHARGE --> STARTUP_HOLD_CLOSE_PRECHARGE: precharge feedback closed
    STARTUP_HOLD_CLOSE_PRECHARGE --> STARTUP_CLOSE_POS: > 90% and ≥ 10 s
    STARTUP_CLOSE_POS --> STARTUP_HOLD_CLOSE_POS: positive closed
    STARTUP_HOLD_CLOSE_POS --> STARTUP_OPEN_PRECHARGE: 100 ms
    STARTUP_OPEN_PRECHARGE --> RUNNING: precharge open
    RUNNING --> ERROR: feedback mismatch
    STARTUP_CLOSE_NEG --> ERROR: wrong feedback
    STARTUP_HOLD_CLOSE_NEG --> ERROR: wrong feedback
    STARTUP_CLOSE_PRECHARGE --> ERROR: wrong feedback
    STARTUP_HOLD_CLOSE_PRECHARGE --> ERROR: wrong feedback
    STARTUP_CLOSE_POS --> ERROR: wrong feedback
    STARTUP_HOLD_CLOSE_POS --> ERROR: wrong feedback
    ERROR --> SHUTDOWN: command OFF
    RUNNING --> SHUTDOWN: command OFF
    SHUTDOWN --> IDLE: precharge < 10% after more than 5 s

Important details:

  • Feedback is inverted. true means a contactor is open; false means it is closed.
  • Precharge voltage is measured by an FC analog input and averaged to reduce noise.
  • Pack voltage comes from Pack_State; maximum pack voltage comes from Pack_SOC. If a matching pair stops arriving for 500 ms, precharge completion is blocked.
  • A wrong contactor state in most startup steps latches AccumulatorContactorWrongState and enters ERROR. STARTUP_ENSURE_OPEN only waits for all feedback to read open, so a welded contactor there stalls startup without a fault. Missing feedback also just waits.
  • The low-SOC check is commented out.

docs.title: Motors and inverters
docs.text:
The motor coordinator owns two Amk objects, one per inverter, plus a starter state machine for each. Its state is reported in FcStatus.MotorState.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> IDLE
    IDLE --> STARTING: command ENABLED
    STARTING --> SWITCHING_INVERTER_ON: both starters succeed
    STARTING --> ERROR: starter error
    SWITCHING_INVERTER_ON --> RUNNING: LV reports switch closed
    RUNNING --> ERROR: either AMK reports error
    RUNNING --> IDLE: command OFF
    ERROR --> IDLE: command OFF

The AMK state machine is the low-level per-inverter sequence:

OFF → SYSTEM_READY → STARTUP_bDCON → STARTUP_bENABLE
    → STARTUP_bINVERTER → STARTUP_X140 → RUNNING

The starter layer waits for the inverter's ready and DC-on acknowledgments before moving through the AMK states. Both motors must reach STARTUP_X140 before the FC asks the LV controller to close the shared inverter switch. The FC proceeds to RUNNING when LvStatus.MotorControllerSwitchClosed is true.

While running, the FC sends each inverter a setpoint frame containing enable bits, a speed request and positive/negative torque limits. Feedback arrives in Inv1/2_ActualValues1/2.

docs.title: Driver inputs and torque
docs.text:
The FC reads two accelerator pedal sensors, brake pressure, steering angle, four wheel-speed inputs, suspension travel and the precharge monitor.

Driver torque is computed at 100 Hz:

Condition Result Both APPS sensors disagree by more than 10% Torque request = 0; AppsImplausible alert APPS above 25% while brake is pressed Torque request = 0 until APPS falls below 5% (EV47Active) Otherwise Request = main APPS percentage

IsBrakePressed() uses the FC's own brake sensor and a threshold of 10%. This is the brake check that lets the governor enter RUNNING.

The pedal request then goes through the active pedal map (linear by default, quadratic available) and into vehicle dynamics. Dynamics produces a left and right request with opposite speed signs; the torque limits are what actually restrict drive torque. Torque vectoring is disabled and the traction-control scale factor is currently fixed at 1.

docs.text: Output Controlled by Accumulator contactors ContactorCommand over vehicle CAN Inverter enable, speed and torque Inv1/2_Setpoints1 over powertrain CAN Shared inverter switch request InverterSwitchCommand over vehicle CAN Brake light request LvCommand.BrakeLightEnable over vehicle CAN Dashboard power DASHBOARD_HSD_EN GPIO, set high at boot Ready-to-drive sound RTDS_EN GPIO, on for ~2 s after entering RUNNING IMD and BMS warning LEDs GPIOs mirrored from LvAlerts; default on if no alert frame Debug LED Toggled at 10 Hz HSD current sensing GPIO mux and ADC sampled locally; values are not transmitted

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
The FC sends FcAlerts with bits for pedal plausibility, accumulator state, motor start/run errors, dashboard boot timeout, CAN errors, missing inverter CAN and HSD overcurrent. The HSD overcurrent bit is always false in this revision. FcStatus carries the governor, accumulator, motor and per-inverter states plus a DBC-valid flag.

The DBC-valid flag compares the FC's generated hash with the LV controller's hash. It is telemetry only; it does not block startup.

docs.title: LV controller
docs.text:
The LV controller (LV) is the power-sequencing board. It enables low-voltage power to the other ECUs and subsystems, controls the inverter supply and shared inverter switch, and manages the status indicator, cooling and brake light.

It has its own power governor. This is not the same state machine as the front controller's global governor: the LV decides when power is available, and the FC decides when HV and torque are allowed.

    READY_TO_DRIVE --> SHUTDOWN_PUMP_OFF: all contactors open
    SHUTDOWN_PUMP_OFF --> SHUTDOWN_FAN_OFF: 50 ms
    SHUTDOWN_FAN_OFF --> PWRUP_ACCUMULATOR_ON: 50 ms
State Main action Leaves when PWRUP_START Everything off; FC, IMU/GPS, pumps and shutdown circuit low 50 ms PWRUP_TSSI_ON TSSI enabled 50 ms PWRUP_PERIPHERALS_ON FC and IMU/GPS power on 50 ms and any LvCommand received PWRUP_ACCUMULATOR_ON Accumulator electronics enabled BMS says all contactors are open PWRUP_MOTOR_CONTROLLER_PRECHARGING Inverter supply enabled Motor-controller state is not ON PWRUP_SHUTDOWN_ON Shutdown circuit enabled Accumulator reports RUNNING DCDC_ON DCDC control is currently commented out 100 ms POWERTRAIN_PUMP_ON Both cooling pumps on 100 ms POWERTRAIN_FAN_ON Fan setpoint 100% At setpoint or 10 s READY_TO_DRIVE No new action; LV power is ready All contactors open SHUTDOWN_PUMP_OFF Pumps off 50 ms SHUTDOWN_FAN_OFF Fan setpoint 0% 50 ms, then back to accumulator startup

READY_TO_DRIVE means the LV power sequence is ready. It does not grant motor torque; that is the FC global governor's decision.

SHUTDOWN_DRIVER_WARNING and SHUTDOWN_COMPLETE exist in the DBC but have no active incoming path in this revision.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: Module Responsibility Accumulator Enables accumulator electronics; reads contactor feedback; reports all-open/running Motor_Controller Controls inverter precharge, main supply and shared switch; reports its state and switch position TSSI Red/green status indicator; reads IMD and BMS fault inputs; red flashes on fault Fans PWM ramp for powertrain cooling; enable outputs are currently forced low HSD Six high-side drivers, 14 current-sense channels; sets HsdOvercurrent Brake light Mirrors LvCommand.BrakeLightEnable to a GPIO; defaults on if no command Suspension Reads rear travel sensors 3 and 4 and sends SuspensionTravel34 DCDC Low-voltage DC/DC measurement and control; not called by the current application Scheduler Fixed-period task table for 100 Hz, 10 Hz and 1 Hz work

docs.title: Inverter supply and switch
docs.text:
The motor-controller module has its own small state machine:

OFF → PRECHARGING (2 s) → PRECHARGING_HANDOFF (50 ms) → ON

It drives three GPIOs: precharge enable, main supply enable and the shared inverter switch. The switch follows InverterSwitchCommand.CloseInverterSwitch from the FC; if no command has been received, the switch is opened.

GetSwitchClosed() returns the requested software value, not an independent physical switch feedback. The FC treats this as the acknowledgment that lets the motors enter RUNNING.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Output Purpose Front-controller power Powers the FC IMU/GPS power Powers navigation peripherals Accumulator electronics power Powers the BMS/accumulator electronics Shutdown-circuit enable Arms the hardware shutdown path Inverter precharge, main supply and switch Brings the inverters online Cooling pump 1/2, fan 1/2, fan PWM Powertrain cooling TSSI enable, red and green High-voltage status indicator Brake light Driver brake lamp HSD enable/select lines Multiplexed current sensing VICOR enable DC/DC control (present but unused by the application)

docs.title: Scheduling and boot status
docs.text:
The LV application is not executable as written

In this revision main() does not call Initialize(), so the HAL, clocks, GPIO, ADC, CAN and timer setup are skipped. The scheduler is also called once with a timestamp that is never refreshed, so registered tasks cannot continue on advancing time. The state diagram above describes the intended governor logic, not a verified boot on hardware.

Constructor-order issues also affect the fan PWM and motor-controller enable lines.

Even with a working scheduler, PWRUP_MOTOR_CONTROLLER_PRECHARGING advances while the motor-controller state is not ON, so it does not wait for the inverter precharge to complete.

docs.title: Software layout
docs.text:
The repository has three top-level code areas:

racecar/
├── projects/        one folder per ECU (the application)
├── lib/             shared code used by the applications
└── scripts/         build, CAN, flashing and logging tools

Each of the four ECUs is a PlatformIO project with one C++ entry point, Src/app.cc. There is no separate bindings or platforms folder in the production ECUs: the application constructs its objects directly and talks to hardware through the shared periph interfaces.

docs.title: One ECU project
docs.text:
projects/front_controller/
├── Src/
│   ├── app.cc           application: objects, main(), tasks or scheduler
│   ├── main.c           CubeMX reset/clock support
│   ├── adc.c can.c gpio.c ...
│   └── stm32f7xx_*.c   CubeMX HAL and interrupt support
├── Inc/                 CubeMX headers, thresholds, tuning, generated CAN
├── lib/                 symlinks to the shared libraries this ECU uses
├── config.yaml          which DBC and CAN node to generate
└── platformio.ini       build environment and source selection

CubeMX still owns the low-level setup: clocks, pin modes, ADC/timer handles and interrupts. The FC, dashboard and TMS applications call those MX_*_Init() functions from Initialize() inside app.cc, then start their scheduled work. The LV controller defines Initialize() but does not call it in this revision (see LV controller).

docs.title: Shared libraries
docs.text:
The shared code is split by purpose:

Library Purpose lib/fc_common/ Front-controller logic: accumulator, motors/AMK, driver interface, vehicle dynamics, suspension, alerts lib/lv_common/ LV module implementations: inverter supply, cooling fans, TSSI, brake light, HSD sensing, scheduler lib/tms_common/ TMS logic: temperature sensor conversion, BMS broadcast, fan controller lib/periph/ Platform-independent interfaces: analog input/output, digital I/O, PWM, CAN lib/mcal/stm32f/ STM32F implementation of periph lib/mcal/linux/, cli/, sil/ Host, terminal and simulation implementations lib/can/, lib/atomic_buffer/ Raw CAN frames, typed bus wrapper and latest-value receive buffer lib/lookup_table/, moving_average/, sls095/, cobs/ Small reusable algorithms and encodings

A project does not copy these libraries. It has symlinks in projects/<ecu>/lib/ that point back to the repository lib/ folder. PlatformIO follows the symlinks and builds only what the project references.

flowchart TB
    App["Application<br/>Src/app.cc + lib/<ecu>_common"]
    Periph["Peripheral interfaces<br/>lib/periph"]
    Mcal["Platform implementation<br/>lib/mcal/stm32f · linux · cli · sil"]
    HW["STM32 peripherals or host"]

    App --> Periph --> Mcal --> HW

This is why the same control code can be unit-tested or run against host adapters without changing the application. On the car, only the STM32 implementation is linked.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Tests live next to the library they cover, for example:

lib/lookup_table/test/test_lookup_table.cc
lib/moving_average/test/test_moving_average.cc
lib/sls095/test/test_sls095.cc

lib/fc_common/test/ also contains a vehicle-dynamics test, but that library has no native environment, so CI does not run it.

Run a library's native tests with PlatformIO:

pio test -d lib/lookup_table -e native

The tests are numerical and host-side. They do not replace a hardware test of CAN timing, GPIO wiring or contactor feedback.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Build one ECU from its project folder:

cd projects/front_controller
pio run -e vehicle

Upload it with an ST-Link attached:

pio run -e vehicle -t upload

The vehicle environment targets the real board. The other environments that appear in older demo projects (cli, linux) are development aids and are not used by the four vehicle ECUs.

docs.title: CAN code generation
docs.text:
Each project's config.yaml names the DBC files and the node this ECU plays:

canGen:
  outputPath: Inc/generated/can
  busses:
    - name: veh
      node: FC
      dbcFile: "../veh.dbc"
    - name: pt
      node: FC
      dbcFile: "../pt.dbc"

The cangen tool is a PlatformIO library dependency, so generated headers are refreshed automatically before a build. Output goes to Inc/generated/can/ and contains only the transmit and receive types for that node. See CAN communication.

docs.title: Demos
docs.text: projects/demo/ contains small teaching projects. Some still use the older main.cc + bindings + platforms/ structure. They are useful for learning PlatformIO and peripherals, but they are not part of the four-ECU firmware.

docs.title: Startup and the global governor
docs.text:
Startup is a conversation, not one state machine. The dashboard reports what the driver is asking for; the front controller decides whether to act; the accumulator, inverters and LV controller do the physical work.

Layer Responsibility Dashboard Shows prompts and sends the driver's requested next step in DashStatus Front controller governor Owns the overall startup state and decides when HV, motors and torque are allowed FC accumulator Sequences the three contactors and monitors feedback FC motors Runs the two AMK inverter startup sequences LV controller Powers the ECUs, accumulator electronics and inverter supply; closes the shared inverter switch TMS Reports temperatures; not part of the startup handshake

docs.title: Global governor
docs.text:
This is the front controller's top-level state machine. It is the single source of truth for whether the car is allowed to drive.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> START_DASHBOARD
    START_DASHBOARD --> WAIT_DRIVER_SELECT: Dash LOGO or SELECT_PROFILE
    WAIT_DRIVER_SELECT --> WAIT_START_HV: Dash WAIT_SELECTION_ACK
    WAIT_START_HV --> STARTING_HV: Dash STARTING_HV
    STARTING_HV --> WAIT_START_MOTOR: Accumulator RUNNING
    STARTING_HV --> ERROR: Accumulator ERROR
    WAIT_START_MOTOR --> STARTING_MOTORS: Dash STARTING_MOTORS
    STARTING_MOTORS --> STARTUP_SEND_READY_TO_DRIVE: Motors RUNNING
    STARTING_MOTORS --> ERROR: Motors ERROR
    STARTUP_SEND_READY_TO_DRIVE --> RUNNING: FC brake > 10%
    RUNNING --> ERROR: Accumulator or motors ERROR
    RUNNING --> SHUTDOWN: Dash SHUTDOWN
    ERROR --> SHUTDOWN: Dash SHUTDOWN
    SHUTDOWN --> START_DASHBOARD: Accumulator IDLE

State numbers come from FcStatus.State in veh.dbc. Value 1 is unused.

State Value FC outputs Advances when Fault behavior START_DASHBOARD 0 Accumulator OFF, motors OFF, torque 0 Dashboard reports LOGO or SELECT_PROFILE After 10 s, sets DashboardBootTimeout alert but keeps waiting WAIT_DRIVER_SELECT 2 OFF, OFF, torque 0 Dashboard reports WAIT_SELECTION_ACK; profile is stored No timeout WAIT_START_HV 3 OFF, OFF, torque 0 Dashboard reports STARTING_HV No timeout STARTING_HV 4 Accumulator ENABLED, motors OFF, torque 0 Accumulator reaches RUNNING Accumulator ERROR → ERROR WAIT_START_MOTOR 5 Accumulator ENABLED, motors OFF, torque 0 Dashboard reports STARTING_MOTORS Does not check accumulator error here STARTING_MOTORS 6 Both ENABLED, torque 0 Motors reach RUNNING Motors ERROR → ERROR; does not check accumulator error here STARTUP_SEND_READY_TO_DRIVE 7 Both ENABLED, torque 0 FC's own brake reading is above 10% No timeout and no subsystem-error check RUNNING 8 Both ENABLED, driver torque allowed Stays until error or shutdown Accumulator/motor ERROR → ERROR; dashboard SHUTDOWN → SHUTDOWN SHUTDOWN 9 OFF, OFF, torque 0 Accumulator reaches IDLE Waits for the accumulator only ERROR 10 OFF, OFF, torque 0 Dashboard reports SHUTDOWN No automatic recovery

The ready-to-drive speaker turns on after entering RUNNING and stays on for about 2 seconds. Torque is not held at zero during that time.

The interlock branch is inactive

There is a local hvil_interrupt check after the governor switch, but the variable is always false in this revision. It creates no transition. The physical shutdown circuit is separate from this software path.

docs.title: Driver and dashboard handshake
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Driver
    participant Dash as Dashboard
    participant FC as Front controller
    participant Acc as FC accumulator
    participant Motors as FC motors
    participant LV as LV controller

    Driver->>Dash: Select profile and confirm
    Dash->>FC: DashStatus = WAIT_SELECTION_ACK + profile
    FC->>FC: WAIT_DRIVER_SELECT → WAIT_START_HV
    FC-->>Dash: DashCommand.ConfigReceived = true

    Driver->>Dash: ENTER at "press for HV"
    Dash->>FC: DashStatus = STARTING_HV
    FC->>Acc: ENABLED
    Acc-->>FC: accumulator RUNNING
    FC->>FC: STARTING_HV → WAIT_START_MOTOR
    FC-->>Dash: DashCommand.HvStarted = true

    Driver->>Dash: ENTER with brake pressed
    Dash->>FC: DashStatus = STARTING_MOTORS
    FC->>Motors: ENABLED
    FC->>LV: InverterSwitchCommand.CloseInverterSwitch
    LV-->>FC: LvStatus.MotorControllerSwitchClosed
    Motors-->>FC: motors RUNNING
    FC->>FC: STARTING_MOTORS → STARTUP_SEND_READY_TO_DRIVE
    FC-->>Dash: DashCommand.MotorStarted = true

    Driver->>FC: Brake pedal above 10%
    FC->>FC: STARTUP_SEND_READY_TO_DRIVE → RUNNING
    FC-->>Dash: DashCommand.DriveStarted = true

DashCommand is a set of repeated level bits, not one-shot events:

Bit True when ConfigReceived FC governor is in WAIT_START_HV HvStarted Accumulator is RUNNING MotorStarted Motor coordinator is RUNNING DriveStarted FC governor is in RUNNING Reset FC governor is in START_DASHBOARD Errored FC governor is in ERROR HvShutdown FC governor is in SHUTDOWN

docs.title: Dashboard state machine
docs.text:
The dashboard's screen state is the driver's request. It is sent over CAN every loop, including while driving.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SELECT_PROFILE
    SELECT_PROFILE --> CONFIRM_SELECTION: ENTER
    CONFIRM_SELECTION --> SELECT_PROFILE: CHANGE, then ENTER
    CONFIRM_SELECTION --> WAIT_SELECTION_ACK: CONFIRM, then ENTER
    WAIT_SELECTION_ACK --> PRESS_FOR_HV: ConfigReceived
    PRESS_FOR_HV --> STARTING_HV: ENTER
    STARTING_HV --> PRESS_FOR_MOTOR: HvStarted
    PRESS_FOR_MOTOR --> STARTING_MOTORS: ENTER + brake > 0.20
    STARTING_MOTORS --> BRAKE_TO_START: MotorStarted
    BRAKE_TO_START --> RUNNING: DriveStarted
    ERROR --> SHUTDOWN: ENTER held > 3000 ms
    SHUTDOWN --> SELECT_PROFILE: Reset
    RUNNING --> SELECT_PROFILE: Reset

LOGO exists in the DBC but is never selected by the dashboard, which boots directly into SELECT_PROFILE.

Global Reset: after the active screen updates, Display::Update() checks DashCommand.Reset. If it is true and the dashboard is not already in SELECT_PROFILE, it forces SELECT_PROFILE.

The error and shutdown screens are incomplete

No normal screen transition enters ERROR, and the running screen has no shutdown action. The FC sends DashCommand.Errored and HvShutdown, but the dashboard does not consume either bit. The error screen's hold-ENTER-to-shutdown path is therefore not reachable through the normal driver flow.

docs.title: What happens underneath
docs.text:
The governor only requests; two FC modules do the physical work:

  • Accumulator: ensure all contactors open, close negative, close precharge, wait for more than 90% and at least 10 s, close positive, then open precharge. Contactor feedback is inverted, and a wrong or missing state can fault or stall the sequence.
  • Motors: start both AMK inverters. When both reach the X140 handoff, the FC asks the LV controller to close the shared inverter switch. The LV reports its requested switch state, and the motors enter RUNNING.

See Front controller for the detailed state diagrams and fault paths.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
Context Nominal period Startup-relevant work FC control task 10 ms (100 Hz) Sensors, governor, accumulator, dynamics, motors, commands FC status task 100 ms (10 Hz) FcStatus, DashCommand, alerts, diagnostics FC identity task 1000 ms (1 Hz) Git revision Dashboard loop 20 ms delay + work Buttons, active screen, DashStatus LV tasks 10 / 100 / 1000 ms intended Governor, modules, status (see the LV scheduler note) TMS tasks 100 / 1000 ms Temperature reporting, fan-duty calculation, Git revision

Key delays and thresholds:

Item Value Minimum precharge time 10 s Precharge complete > 90% of pack voltage Contactor step hold 100 ms Pack voltage data timeout 500 ms Shutdown discharge complete < 10% after > 5 s FC brake-to-drive threshold > 10% Dashboard brake-to-start threshold > 0.20 percentage points Dashboard boot alert > 10 s Ready-to-drive speaker ~2 s

The FC's elapsed counters are software counters incremented by 10 per 100 Hz update. They are not wall-clock deadlines, and a late task does not change the increment.

Most governor waits have no timeout. If the dashboard stops sending, its last DashStatus remains valid and can still drive a transition because there is no sender-age check. Missing contactor feedback or a missing LvStatus likewise leaves the relevant state machine waiting. The pack-voltage check is the main exception at 500 ms.

docs.title: Shutdown and restart
docs.text:
A dashboard SHUTDOWN request is accepted in RUNNING and ERROR. The FC then:

  1. commands the accumulator and motors OFF;
  2. the accumulator opens all three contactors;
  3. the accumulator waits for precharge below 10% and more than 5 seconds, then reports IDLE;
  4. the FC returns to START_DASHBOARD.

DashCommand.Reset is true while the FC is in START_DASHBOARD, so the dashboard returns to profile selection. The dashboard remains powered throughout; its power is controlled by the FC GPIO, not by this state machine.

The physical shutdown circuit can remove power independently of any of these software states. This repository documents the software requests and feedback it can observe, not the complete electrical response of that circuit.

docs.title: TMS
docs.text: The thermal management system (TMS) is the simplest ECU. It reads six accumulator thermistors, filters them, reports temperatures on vehicle CAN, and computes the accumulator cooling-fan duty. The fan PWM output is not actually started in this revision. The TMS does not participate in the startup handshake and has no startup/fault governor of its own.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
Task Period Work task_10hz 100 ms Read and filter six sensors; send BmsBroadcast and TMSValues; update fan duty; toggle debug LEDs; handle CAN-flash request task_1hz 1000 ms Send TmsGitHash

Both are FreeRTOS tasks with static stacks. The application starts them and then starts the scheduler.

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Six ADC voltages] --> B[Voltage-to-temperature<br/>lookup table]
    B --> C[20-sample moving average]
    C --> D[Min / max / average]
    D --> E[BmsBroadcast to BMS]
    C --> F[TMSValues diagnostic frame]
    C --> G[Average of six sensors]
    G --> H[Temperature-to-fan-power<br/>lookup]
    H --> I[Inverse PWM duty<br/>20%/s slew limit]
    I --> J[Fan PWM on TIM4]

docs.title: Temperature measurement
docs.text:
Each sensor is connected to an ADC channel and converted with a lookup table from the sensor datasheet. Readings outside the table clamp to its endpoints. There is no open/short detection or per-sensor validity flag.

Each sensor then passes through a 20-sample moving average. The average is preloaded with zeros and always divides by 20, so the first samples are biased toward zero: a constant 40 °C input reads about 2 °C on the first sample and reaches 40 °C after twenty samples.

docs.title: BmsBroadcast — every 100 ms
docs.text:
This eight-byte frame mimics an Orion thermistor module:

Field Meaning ThermModuleNum Module 0 LowThermValue, HighThermValue Lowest and highest integer temperature AvgThermValue Integer mean temperature NumThermEn 6 HighThermID, LowThermID Zero-based sensor indices Checksum Sum of the logical bytes plus 0x41, truncated to 8 bits

The BMS consumes this frame as if it came from its own thermistor module.

docs.title: TMSValues — every 100 ms
docs.text: A six-byte diagnostic frame with one value per sensor. Each field is built as static_cast<uint8_t>(temperature × 50). At normal positive temperatures this exceeds the 8-bit range, so this frame is not a reliable Celsius representation as implemented.

docs.title: TmsGitHash — every 1 second
docs.text: Commit hash and dirty flag. Unlike the FC and LV, the TMS application does not send a DBC hash.

docs.title: Fan control
docs.text:
The fan power is based on the mean of all six filtered temperatures:

Mean temperature Requested fan power ≤ 19 °C 0% 19–20 °C Linear 0 → 30% 20–50 °C Linear 30 → 100% ≥ 50 °C 100%

The fan input uses inverse logic, so the PWM duty is 100 - power. Duty changes by at most 20 percentage points per second, which is 2 points per 100 ms update. Because the mean is used, one hot sensor can be diluted by five cooler ones.

The fan controller has a Start() method that both starts the PWM timer and sets the initial duty. In this revision the application never calls it, and MX_TIM4_Init() configures the timer but does not start the output. The periodic duty writes alone do not produce an active PWM signal.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Function Pin Thermistors 1–6 ADC1 channels 10–15, PC0–PC5 Fan PWM TIM4 channel 1, PB6 Debug green PE2 Debug red PA3 Vehicle CAN CAN2

The clock is 96 MHz system / 48 MHz APB1, and CAN is configured for 500 kbit/s.

docs.title: Build and tools
docs.text: Everything needed to build, test, flash and observe the car lives in the repository. The four ECU projects share the same build model; the supporting tools are separate.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• PlatformIO Core (pio) for the ECU firmware.
  • Python 3.13+ for the CAN tools and documentation.
  • An ST-Link for wired flashing.

PlatformIO downloads the STM32 toolchain, framework and libraries on the first build.

docs.title: Build and upload an ECU
docs.text:
Run PlatformIO from the project directory. Each production project has a vehicle environment for the real board:

Project PlatformIO board Environment projects/front_controller Nucleo-F767ZI vehicle projects/lvcontroller Nucleo-F767ZI vehicle projects/dashboard STM32F469I Discovery vehicle projects/tms Nucleo-F767ZI vehicle

The board names are PlatformIO definitions. The FC, LV controller and TMS run on custom STM32F767 boards; only the dashboard is a Discovery kit.

cd projects/front_controller
pio run -e vehicle              # build
pio run -e vehicle -t upload    # build and flash

The build regenerates CAN headers, compiles the CubeMX startup code and links the shared libraries through the project's lib/ symlinks. The Git hash is embedded at build time and sent over CAN by the FC, LV controller and TMS. The dashboard defines a Git-hash message but does not send it.

Demo projects under projects/demo/ have additional host environments (such as cli and linux) for teaching and simulation. They are not part of the vehicle firmware.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Host-side unit tests live in the library's test/ folder and run in the library's native environment:

pio test --project-dir lib/lookup_table
pio test --project-dir lib/moving_average
pio test --project-dir lib/sls095

The tests cover numerical code such as lookup tables, moving averages and the SLS095 encoder. There are no automated hardware-in-the-loop tests in this repository.

Continuous integration builds every project with a vehicle environment and runs the tests of every library that has a test/ folder and a platformio.ini.

docs.title: Static analysis
docs.text:
pio check is configured to use clang-tidy:

pio check --project-dir projects/front_controller \
  --flags "--checks=bugprone-*,clang-analyzer-*,google-*,performance-*" \
  --fail-on-defect=high

scripts/static_analysis/static_analysis.sh runs the same check for projects with changed files.

docs.title: CAN code generation
docs.text:
scripts/cangen reads a project's config.yaml and the DBC files, then generates C++ message and bus classes into Inc/generated/can/.

canGen:
  outputPath: Inc/generated/can
  busses:
    - name: veh
      node: FC
      dbcFile: "../veh.dbc"

cangen is registered as a PlatformIO library dependency, so the headers are regenerated automatically before every build. To regenerate by hand:

cd scripts/cangen
poetry install
poetry run cangen ../../projects/front_controller

The generated code is written for one node at a time. The front controller gets vehicle and powertrain messages; the LV and TMS get vehicle messages only.

docs.title: Watch the CAN buses
docs.text:
The two monitor scripts configure a SocketCAN interface at 500 kbit/s and open cantools monitor with the matching DBC:

cd projects
bash monitor_veh.sh    # vehicle bus, can1, veh.dbc
bash monitor_pt.sh     # powertrain bus, can0, pt.dbc

They require Linux, iproute2 and cantools. The interface names can0 and can1 are local conventions. The DAQ setup uses the opposite naming, so check which channel is wired to which bus before trusting a dump.

scripts/can_errgo/ provides a terminal interface for watching and acknowledging CAN errors on a virtual or physical interface.

docs.title: Flash over CAN
docs.text:
scripts/canflash/ runs a web server on the Raspberry Pi inside the car. With the Pi powered and on its local network, open http://192.168.12.1:8000/, choose an ECU, choose a firmware binary and start the flash.

  • Supported targets in the web interface: front controller, LV controller, TMS.
  • The dashboard is not flashed through this tool.
  • Flashing uses the STM32 CAN bootloader; the Pi controls each ECU's boot pin.
  • In this revision only the TMS application checks for the CAN-flash request, so validate the other two targets before relying on them.
  • The server starts automatically on the Pi. See scripts/canflash/README.md for running it locally.

docs.title: Data acquisition
docs.text:
scripts/daq/ is the separate telemetry stack that runs on the Raspberry Pi:

vehicle + powertrain CAN
        │
        ▼
logger.py → CSV on the SD card
        └──→ InfluxDB Cloud → Grafana on the dock laptop

It reads raw frames, decodes selected signals with the same DBC files, writes decoded rows to CSV and uploads key values over cellular. See scripts/daq/README.md for the Pi setup, the Linux VM test setup and the Grafana dashboard. There are two installers: setup_pi.sh for the cloud deployment and setup.sh for a local InfluxDB/Grafana install.

The DAQ is not part of the ECU firmware and does not affect vehicle control.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs Material:

cd docs
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve     # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
.venv/bin/mkdocs build     # generate site/ for deployment

Install the Python requirements from docs/requirements.txt if the virtual environment does not exist yet. The GitHub Actions workflow builds and deploys the site when changes reach main.

docs.title: Calculating CAN Traffic
docs.text: In order to calculate the CAN load, we must define a few variables related to the CAN protocol.

docs.title: Baud
docs.text: The baud rate is the rate at which data is transfered in a communication channel (like CAN). For example, 9600 Baud rate is 9600 bits per second

docs.title: Frequency
docs.text:
The frequency of a message, expressed in (Hz), is how often a message is transmitted per second. Different messages can have different frequencies.

This variation affects the total bits transmitted and, in turn, the bus load. To calculate bits per second, consider each message’s frequency and whether their lengths differ.

docs.title: Message Length
docs.text:
The message length in a CAN frame can be calculated as a function of the data length. This calculation includes several fixed fields and a variable data field, which changes based on the message's data content.

Standard CAN frame bit composition.Adapted from CSS Electronics

Each CAN frame consists of several fields with fixed bit lengths, plus a variable-length data field. The total frame length is:

\[ 1 + 11 + 1 + 6 + 8x + 16 + 2 + 7 = 44 + 8x \text{ bits}\]

where \(x\) represents the number of bytes in the data field.

docs.title: Total CAN Traffic
docs.text:
We must multiply total bits per second by 1.2 to account for bit stuffing

\[\begin{align} \text{Total Bits Per Second} &= 1.2 \times \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\text{Frequency}_i \times \text{Message Length}_i \right) \end{align}\]

docs.title: Total Bus Load
docs.text: \[\begin{align} \text{Bus Load}\% = \frac{\text{Total Bits per Second}}{\text{Baud Rate}} \times 100\% \end{align}\]

docs.title: Sample calculation
docs.text:
Given:

Baud Rate: 500 kbaud (500,000 bits transferred per second)

Message Type Data Length Frequency (Hz) Message Length (Bits) Battery Status 8 100 \(44 + 8 \times 8 = 108\) Motor Control 5 50 \(44 + 8 \times 5 = 84\) \[\begin{align} \text{Total Bits Per Second} &= 1.2 \times \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\text{Frequency}_i \times \text{Message Length}_i \right)\\ \text{Total Bits Per Second} &= 1.2 \times \left((100\text{ Hz} \times 108\text{ bits}) + (50\text{ Hz} \times 84\text{ bits})\right)\\ &= 1.2 \times \left(10800 + 4200\right)\text{ bits per second}\\ &= 1.2 \times 15000\text{ bits per second}\\ &= 18000\text{ bits per second} \end{align}\]

The bus load is the previous example can be calculated as:

\[ \text{Bus Load}\% = \frac{\text{Total Bits per Second}}{\text{Baud Rate}} \times 100\% \] \[ \text{Bus Load} = \left(\frac{18000}{500000}\right) \times 100\% = 3.60\% \]

docs.title: Visual Studio Code
docs.text: Install it from https://code.visualstudio.com/Download.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Install the latest Python from https://www.python.org/downloads/. We require version 3.13 or newer. When prompted, add Python to your PATH.

Verify its installation by running

python --version # on windows
python3 --version # on Linux/Mac

docs.title: PlatformIO
docs.text:
PlatformIO is a VS Code extension which provides cross-platform support for embedded-systems development.

Follow the PlatformIO IDE installation instructions at https://platformio.org/platformio-ide.

Install the "Native" platform dependencies https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/platforms/native.html.

Optional: You may also install PlatformIO Core for CLI support.

Note on C++ Extensions

The PlatformIO VS Code extension will automatically install the C/C++ extension to provide language support.

Prior to 2025-26, Mac Formula used Clangd for C++ language support. You should disable/uninstall the Clangd extension when working on racecar.

docs.title: STM32CubeMX
docs.text:
CubeMX is a program which generates configuration code for our microcontrollers.

  1. Go to www.st.com, click on the account icon in the top right and create an account. You will need this username and password later on.

  2. Download and install STM32CubeMX version 6.15.0 from https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubemx.html.

Warning

You must install exactly version 6.15.0 (not even 6.15.1). Using a different version than your team members will cause conflicts when opening files.

docs.title: Git & GitHub
docs.text:
1. Create a GitHub account https://github.com/. As a student, you should join GitHub Education https://github.com/education to get benefits like increased storage and free GitHub Actions.

  2. Install Git from https://git-scm.com/downloads.

  3. (Windows only) Enable symbolic links.

    1. Enable "Developer Mode" https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/get-started/enable-your-device-for-development
    2. Run git config --global core.symlinks true
Git Bash (for Windows only)

Git Bash is an alternative terminal shell which is installed alongside git. This shell emulates the Linux bash shell, allowing you to use commands like grep, ls, rm and many more on Windows.

If you are on Windows, you must use Git Bash as your shell when developing in racecar/. (i.e. not Command Prompt or Powershell).

In VS Code, you can change your default shell by pressing F1 and entering >Terminal: Select Default Profile and selecting Git Bash.

docs.title: Clone the racecar Repository
docs.text:
Find our repository on GitHub https://github.com/macformula/racecar.

Copy the repository address:

Navigate to a directory where you want to hold the racecar repo, then run

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/macformula/racecar.git

Choosing a folder

Good locations are short and memorable. Consider C:\formula\ on Windows or ~/formula on Linux/Mac.

Do not use a directory that has spaces anywhere in its path, such as C:\Users\My Files\Formula. Spaces wreak havoc on automated scripts.

Automated Backups

Never put Git repo somehwere that is automatically backed-up by another program (ex. OneDrive).

Git is itself a backup system, so it will fight with OneDrive and corrupt your local repository.

docs.text:

pip install pre-commit

Now go to the racecar/ folder and run

pre-commit install

docs.title: Connect to the Board
docs.text:
Development Boards + DashboardVehicle ECUs

Most development boards (such as the Nucleo-144 and dashboard kit) have built-in ST-Link hardware and a USB interface.

Simply connect the board to your laptop with a USB cable.

ST-Link on Nucleo-144 F767ZI

The vehicle ECUs are not development boards. They are bare STM32F7 processors soldered to a circuit board. These boards do not have a built-in ST-Link or USB interface so we must use a different connector.

You will need and external ST-Link and a USB cable from the blue tool chest in the Hatch bay. Some of the ST-Links are Micro-USB and others are USB-C. We should have cables for both.

ST-Link and cables are kept in bags in this drawer. Return them when finished!

Please wrap the ST-Link in electrical tape since it has exposed conductors and is very easy to fry.

E-Tape would have prevented the Great ST-Link Massacre of Comp '24.

  1. Ensure the ECU is off (not receiving power) and the USB is not connected to your laptop.

  2. Carefully connect the grey ribbon cable to the ST-Link and the JTAG connector on the ECU board.

    Both ends of the ribbon cable have a tab which must align with the notch on the connector.

    Connector tab and notch

  3. Power on the ECU. Talk to an upper year SW or Electrical member for help.

  4. Connect your laptop to the ST-Link using the USB cable.

Full setup

ST-Link issue for Mac Users

For some reason, ST-Links don't work when directly connected to a Mac. You need to use a USB hub to indirectly connect to it.

flowchart LR
    Mac --> USB[USB Hub]
    USB --> ST-Link

docs.title: Upload with PlatformIO
docs.text: Open a PlatformIO project in VS Code. Select the vehicle environment and click upload.

docs.title: Open a project
docs.text:
Open the PlatformIO Home page from the VS Code status bar () or with F1 → PlatformIO: PlatformIO Home, then choose Open Project and select a folder under projects/.

For the car firmware, open the ECU you are working on, for example projects/front_controller. Each production project contains:

front_controller/
├── Src/              application and CubeMX source
├── Inc/              headers and generated CAN code
├── lib/              symlinks to the shared libraries
├── config.yaml       CAN generation settings
└── platformio.ini    build environments

The application entry point is Src/app.cc. See Software layout for the full repository structure.

docs.title: Select an environment
docs.text:
Use the PlatformIO status-bar menu to choose an environment:

  • vehicle builds for the real board and is the only environment used by the four production ECUs.
  • Demo projects under projects/demo/ may also offer host environments such as cli or linux. These are teaching and simulation aids.

docs.title: Build and upload
docs.text:
Use the PlatformIO buttons in the status bar:

  • Build compiles the selected environment.
  • Upload flashes the board over ST-Link.

The same actions from a terminal:

cd projects/front_controller
pio run -e vehicle
pio run -e vehicle -t upload

A build regenerates the CAN headers from the DBC files and embeds the current Git hash. The first build installs the toolchain and libraries and is slower than later builds.

To connect an ST-Link to a vehicle ECU, see Uploading firmware to STM.

docs.title: Editing this site
docs.text:
We use Material for MkDocs to generate beautiful documentation without worrying about the intricacies of modern web development. The content is written with Markdown which has a low learning curve for anyone not already familiar with it.

The site is hosted with GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text:
These steps only need to be performed once.

  1. Clone the racecar repository.

    git clone https://github.com/macformula/racecar.git

  2. Create a Python virtual environment.

    This step is optional but recommended.

    cd racecar/docs
python -m venv .venv

    Activate the virtual environment.

    WindowsUnix 
    .venv\Scripts\activate

    source .venv/bin/activate

  3. Install the documentation dependencies.

    pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Editing and Viewing the Site
docs.text:
Follow these steps each time you want to edit the site.

This section assumes that you have already activated your virtual environment, if applicable.

  1. Launch an mkdocs server to locally host the site.

    $ cd racecar/docs
$ mkdocs serve
...
INFO    -  [22:01:58] Serving on http://127.0.0.1:8000/

  2. Open the listed URL in your web browser.

    In this example, open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ in a browser.

  3. Edit the contents of the docs/ folder. Your locally hosted site will update whenever you edit and save a relevant file.

    Markdown References

    Generic Markdown https://www.markdownguide.org/cheat-sheet/

    Material for MkDocs https://squidfunk.github.io/mkdocs-material/reference/

docs.title: Publishing Changes
docs.text:
When you are satisfied with your changes, commit and make a pull request.

A Github action will automatically re-build the website when the PR is merged into main. The build artefacts are pushed to the ghpages branch of the repository from which the website is hosted. The website will update within a few minutes.

The action is specified in racecar/.github/workflows/deploy-ghpages.yml and was copied from https://squidfunk.github.io/mkdocs-material/publishing-your-site/.

The ghpages branch

The action force-pushes build artefacts to the ghpages branch, so any changes made on this branch will be overwritten. Edit the contents of racecar/docs to modify the site.

docs.text:

  • Kvaser Drivers https://kvaser.com/download/

    Kvaser drivers are only available for Windows and Linux, so you cannot follow this tutorial on MacOS.

  • The Kvaser USB CAN adapter (which should be kept in the bay).

docs.title: Physical Connections
docs.text:
1. Connect the USB port the Kvaser to your computer.

  2. Connect the D-Sub port of the Kvaser to the CAN port.

    Vehicle CAN PortsTestbench CAN Port

    Located on the underside of the dashboard. One port for the VEH CAN bus and one for POWERTRAIN.

    Only the VEH CAN bus is available.

docs.title: Busmaster Setup
docs.text:
Open Busmaster. Under "Driver Selection" choose "Kvaser CAN."

Under "Channel Configuration," configure a Kvaser channel by selecting it on the left and clicking the >> button. Configure the BaudRate to 500 000 bps.

Kvaser channel numbering

The Kvaser has 2 D-Sub connectors to support 2 CAN channels / busses. The cables are labelled Ch.1 and Ch.2, but they appear in Busmaster configuration as Channel 0 and Channel 1, respectively.

However, once you start reading CAN messages, they are correctly numbered 1 and 2 again (see next image).

Click "Connect" in the top-left to start viewing CAN messages!

The raw binary CAN messages are hard to read. In the next section we will associate a CAN database to allow Busmaster to decode for us.

docs.title: Interpret CAN Messages
docs.text:
Busmaster only accepts a special .dbf database format. Fortunately, it provides a tool to convert our .dbc files to .dbf.

Under "Tools" select "Format Converter."

Go to "Other Converters" and select "DBC to DBF." Choose a .dbc input file and click "Convert." Note the "Output File" destination.

Return to the "CAN" tab and click "Database" → "Associate." Choose the .dbf file.

Under "Message Window" enable "Interpret."

Note

"Interpret" is disabled until a database is associated.

Now look at the Message Window. Each message should have a name (ex. FC_Status) and you can expand the signals by clicking the +.

DBC file corresponding to this screenshot 
BO_ 255 FC_Status: 5 FC
    SG_ GovStatus : 0|8@1+ (1,0) [0|255] "" LVC, PC_SG
    SG_ DiStatus : 8|8@1+ (1,0) [0|255] "" LVC, PC_SG
    SG_ MiStatus : 16|8@1+ (1,0) [0|255] "" LVC, PC_SG
    SG_ BmStatus : 24|8@1+ (1,0) [0|255] "" LVC, PC_SG
    SG_ UserFlag : 32|8@1+ (1,0) [0|255] "" LVC, PC_SG

BO_ 111 LvControllerStatus: 6 LVC
    SG_ LvState : 0|8@1+ (1,0) [0|1] ""  RPI
    SG_ Elapsed : 8|32@1- (1,0) [0|1] ""  RPI
    SG_ Flag : 40|1@1+ (1,0) [0|1] ""  RPI

BO_ 113 SuspensionTravel34: 2 LVC
    SG_ STP3 : 0|8@1+ (1,0) [0|255] "" FC,RPI
    SG_ STP4 : 8|8@1+ (1,0) [0|255] "" FC,RPI

BO_ 257 DashStatus: 1 Dash
    SG_ Status : 0|8@1+ (1,0) [0|255] "" FC

For example:

  • In the DBC, FC_Status has ID 255 which is hex 0x0FF in Busmaster.
  • The Elapsed field is is bits 8-39 of the LvControllerStatus message. The "Data Bytes" are 0x00001F95 which is hex for 8085, matching the interpreted value.

docs.title: Send CAN Messages
docs.text:
Open the "Transmit Window."

Select "Add Message" and choose a message from the database to send.

Warning

If you are using multiple CAN channels, you must configure the "Channel" column to send the message on the right one.

Edit the "Signal Details" to change the signal values.

Click "Send Message" to send it once, or enable "Repetition" to periodically send the message.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Can't transmit over Channel 2

There is a bug in the Transmit Window. If you change the transmit Channel to 2, you will lose the message's database information like its name and signals.

You can still send a message over channel 2 but must manually set the bits in the "Data Byte View."

If you only need to transmit over one channel, connect the Ch.1 D-Sub to that bus to avoid this error.

Channel 1: Message has name and signal breakdown

Channel 2: Message doesn't have name or signals

docs.title: SSH and Commit Signing
docs.text:
This tutorial will guide you through setting up an SSH key and commit signing for GitHub. SSH keys are a more secure way to connect to GitHub, rather than other protocols like HTTPS. Commit signing is used to verify that commits are coming from you and have not been tampered with.

Warning

You must have a verified email address on GitHub to add SSH keys and sign commits.

docs.title: Create an SSH Key
docs.text:
In a bash terminal, enter the following command:

WindowsLinux/Mac 
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_github_email@example.com"

When prompted, save to the default location c:/Users/YOU/.ssh/id_ed25519 and do not enter a passphrase. This will allow you to use the key without entering a password every time you push to GitHub.

Continue with the following commands:

cat c:/Users/YOU/.ssh/id_ed25519 | clip
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add c:/Users/YOU/.ssh/id_ed25519

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_github_email@example.com"

When prompted, save to the default location ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 and do not enter a passphrase. This will allow you to use the key without entering a password every time you push to GitHub.

Continue with the following commands:

pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

To add the key to your GitHub account, go to https://github.com/settings/ssh/new.

  • Name your key something descriptive.
  • Select "Authentication Key" as the key type.
  • Paste the contents of id_ed25519.pub into the "Key" box.
  • Click "Add SSH Key".

Open another terminal to test your connection to GitHub by entering the following command:

ssh -T git@github.com

Type "yes" when it asks if you want to continue connecting. You should see a message like "Hi username! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access."

docs.title: Enable Commit Signing
docs.text:
To add a signing key to your GitHub account, go to https://github.com/settings/ssh/new.

  • Name your key something descriptive.
  • Select "Signing Key" as the key type.
  • Paste the contents of id_ed25519.pub into the "Key" box.
  • Click "Add SSH Key."

Update your git configuration in your terminal to automatically sign commits with your key:

WindowsLinux/Mac 
git config --global user.signingkey c:/Users/YOU/.ssh/id_ed25519
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

docs.title: Enable Vigilant Mode
docs.text:
Go to https://github.com/settings/ssh and scroll down to the "Vigilant Mode" section. Enable "Enable Vigilant Mode".

This will now mark and display all of your commits with a signature verification status tag.

Verify your commits are signed by checking your commit history on GitHub for "Verified" tags.

docs.title: Set Repo to Use SSH
docs.text:
It is likely your repository is using HTTPS to connect to GitHub. To check which remote URL is currently being used, run the following terminal command inside of a repository:

git remote -v

To convert to SSH, run the following command, replacing orgname and reponame with your GitHub organization and repository names (i.e. macformula and racecar):

git remote set-url origin git@github.com:orgname/reponame.git

To avoid this manual configuration in the future, clone repositories using their SSH URL instead of HTTPS.

docs.title: Virtual CAN on WSL2
docs.text:
By default, WSL2 does not support Virtual CAN, however it can be enabled by building a custom WSL2 kernel.

This setup assumes you are running within WSL. If you do not have WSL installed, open up a Windows terminal and run:

wsl --install

docs.title: Step 1: Update the WSL Environment
docs.text:
Run the following commands in your WSL terminal to update your environment and install the required dependencies.

sudo apt-get update -y

docs.title: Install dependencies
docs.text:
sudo apt install -y dwarves libelf-dev flex bison libssl-dev libncurses-dev bc build-essential make
sudo apt install -y --no-install-recommends wslu

docs.title: Step 2: Download the WSL2 Linux Kernel
docs.text:
To ensure compatibility, you need the specific kernel version of WSL2.

  1. Check your kernel version:

    uname -r
    • Example output: 5.15.153.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2
    • Note the version number, as it must match with <your-kernel-version> in step 2, 3, and 4.

  2. Download the kernel source:

    • Go to the WSL2 Linux Kernel repository.
    • Find and copy the link for the Source code (tar.gz) file matching your kernel version.

  3. Download and extract the file:

    wget https://github.com/microsoft/WSL2-Linux-Kernel/archive/refs/tags/linux-msft-wsl-<your-kernel-version>.tar.gz
tar -xf linux-msft-wsl-<your-kernel-version>.tar.gz

  4. Navigate to the extracted folder:

    cd WSL2-Linux-Kernel-<your-kernel-version>

docs.title: Step 3: Configure Kernel Settings
docs.text:
1. Load current configuration:

    cat /proc/config.gz | gunzip > .config

  2. Prepare the kernel for modules:

    make prepare modules_prepare -j $(expr $(nproc) - 1)

  3. Open the configuration menu:

    make menuconfig -j $(expr $(nproc) - 1)

    A menu interface should open. Use this to enable the necessary drivers for Virtual CAN.

docs.title: Enable CAN Drivers
docs.text:
• Navigate to Networking Support and press Enter.
  • Select CAN BUS subsystem support by pressing M, then press Enter.

docs.title: Enable CAN Device Drivers
docs.text:
• Navigate to CAN Device Drivers.
  • For each driver shown in the screenshot, press M to enable as a module.
  • Save and exit the configuration menu.

docs.title: Step 4: Compile and Install Kernel Modules
docs.text:
Run the following commands to compile and install the Virtual CAN modules:

make modules -j $(expr $(nproc) - 1)
sudo make modules_install

Then, compile the kernel:

make -j $(expr $(nproc) - 1)

docs.title: Step 5: Configure WSL to Use the Custom Kernel
docs.text:
1. Create a symbolic link for the module directory, matching your kernel version:

    sudo ln -s /lib/modules/5.15.153.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2+ /lib/modules/5.15.153.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2

  2. Copy the vmlinux file:

    Replace <yourwindowsloginname> with your actual Windows username:

    cp vmlinux /mnt/c/Users/<yourwindowsloginname>/
    • In Windows File Explorer, you should now see a file named vmlinux.

  3. Configure .wslconfig:

    Create a file named .wslconfig in the same directory (i.e. in /mnt/c/Users/<yourwindowsloginname>/) and paste the following to the file:

    [wsl2]
kernel=C:\\Users\\<yourwindowsloginname>\\vmlinux

docs.title: Step 6: Restart WSL and Verify
docs.text:
1. In a separate Windows terminal (not WSL), restart WSL:

    wsl --shutdown

  2. Wait ~10 seconds, then check that WSL has no active processes:

    wsl --list -v

  3. Verify the setup by running WSL again, then execute these commands:

    sudo modprobe can
sudo modprobe can-raw
sudo modprobe vcan

If there is no other message, the installation was successful.
